title: Hancock Taylor, Fincastle surveyor
summary: Virginia deputy surveyor Hancock Taylor worked under Col. William Preston mapping Kentucky bounty land in the early 1770s. He had already been at the Falls of the Ohio in 1769…
bodyMarkdown:
Before Kentucky had counties, it had surveyors. [Hancock Taylor](/people/#hancock-taylor) was one of the first. He was a Virginia deputy surveyor working under Col. [William Preston](/people/#william-preston), the surveyor of Fincastle County, Virginia, which then took in the whole Kentucky country.

Taylor knew the Ohio before most. He was at the [Falls of the Ohio](/stories/falls-of-the-ohio/) in 1769, on his way downriver to New Orleans. By 1773 he was back, surveying in Kentucky for Preston's office.

The work was about land promised to soldiers. Virginia owed bounty land to veterans of the French and Indian War, and Preston's deputies went west to mark out tracts. The lines Taylor and his fellow surveyors ran helped lay the ground for later claims around Louisville and across the Bluegrass.

Surveying was dangerous work. The men carried chains and compasses into country the Shawnee and other nations used as hunting ground and had never given up. By the summer of 1774, tension along the Ohio had turned into Lord Dunmore's War. Preston sent word for his surveyors to come home.

In July 1774 Taylor was near the mouth of the Kentucky River when Native warriors shot him. The [state marker at his grave](https://history.ky.gov/markers/grave-of-hancock-taylor) says he rejoined his party, and his companions carried him toward the settlements. They brought him as far as a spot just south of present-day [Richmond](/stories/richmond-from-millers-barn/), where he died.

They buried him on Taylor's Fork of Silver Creek in what is now Madison County. The stream still carries his name. Taylor died a year before Boonesborough was founded, a few miles away. He was one of the first Virginians to die while surveying in Kentucky.

Surveys like his came before nearly everything else in Kentucky history. Stations, towns, and court fights over land all depended on where lines like his had been run, and on whether anyone could still find the marked trees.

## Kentucky today

State historical marker #1685, "Grave of Hancock Taylor," stands on KY 52 about a mile west of Richmond. It points to the burial place about seven-tenths of a mile east, on Taylor's Fork of Silver Creek. In Richmond, the [Madison County seat story](/stories/richmond-from-millers-barn/) begins just north of where his companions stopped.
Source: [KHS marker #1685: Grave of Hancock Taylor](https://history.ky.gov/markers/grave-of-hancock-taylor)
